chapters.title: Chapter 4: Risk Management and Real-World Implementation

lessons.title: From Backtest to Live Capital: An Implementation Checklist

body.text: A backtest that survives every check in Chapter 3, and a portfolio construction that respects every constraint in this chapter, still is not a live strategy. The gap between 'this would have worked' and 'this is now working with real capital' is where most factor strategies that never had a chance quietly reveal themselves, and where good ones quietly earn the confidence to scale.

children.text: This closing lesson is the practical bridge from everything this course has covered, factor theory in Chapter 1, the individual factors in Chapter 2, construction and backtesting in Chapter 3, exposure and crowding monitoring earlier in this chapter, to actually running a factor strategy with real money.
Paper Trading: The Bridge Between Backtest and Real Capital

markDefs.definition: Running a strategy's actual, live decision process, using real-time data and generating real orders, without committing real capital, to surface operational issues a backtest cannot reveal.

children.text: Even a rigorously point-in-time, bias-free backtest, exactly what Chapter 3 covered, cannot catch everything, because a backtest is fundamentally a historical simulation, not a live operational process.

, running the strategy's actual decision process against real-time data and generating real orders that are simply never sent to a broker, is the step that surfaces problems a backtest structurally cannot: data feed delays and timing mismatches, bugs in the code that computes the factor score under real operational conditions, and whether the rebalancing process, manually or programmatically placing dozens of orders across the NSE within a defined window, is actually feasible on a live trading day rather than just on paper. A reasonable minimum is paper trading through several full rebalance cycles before committing any real capital, so the process has actually been exercised under real, if consequence-free, conditions more than once.

Moving from zero to full intended capital in one step throws away the chance to catch problems while the cost of being wrong is still small. A phased approach, starting with a modest pilot allocation, comparing its realised performance against both the backtest and the paper-trading results, and increasing capital in stages as confidence builds, keeps early mistakes cheap. This also directly tests something Chapter 2's size factor lesson raised: capacity. A strategy's backtested edge, especially one leaning on smaller, less liquid NSE names, can shrink as deployed capital grows and the strategy's own trading starts to move prices against itself, a problem invisible at small scale and only discoverable by actually scaling up and watching what happens to realised costs.
Live Monitoring: Backtest Expectations vs Realised Performance

Once live, the discipline from earlier in this chapter continues: track realised factor exposure and Effective N regularly, not just at rebalancing, and add a direct comparison between live performance and what the backtest would have predicted for the same period, including how the live strategy's drawdown compares to the worst drawdown the backtest ever produced. A live drawdown meaningfully exceeding the backtest's historical worst case is not automatically proof the strategy is broken, markets can always produce something worse than any historical sample, but it is a clear, predefined signal that a formal strategy review is warranted rather than optional.

markDefs.definition: A predefined, written rule specifying the exact conditions under which a live strategy will be paused, de-risked, or shut down, decided before deployment and independent of how the manager feels about the strategy in the moment a breach occurs.

children.text: This is exactly where a written

earns its keep. Chapter 2 closed with a warning about performance chasing, capitulating on a factor at precisely the point of maximum pain, right before a recovery. A kill switch defined and written down before going live, for example, 'pause and formally review the strategy if the live drawdown exceeds 1.5 times the backtest's worst historical drawdown', protects against making that exact decision emotionally, in real time, under the influence of a losing streak. Deciding the rule in advance, while calm and unemotional, is what makes it useful; deciding it after the losses have already started is just performance chasing with extra steps.
The Full Pipeline, Start to Finish

body.title: From Factor Idea to Live, Monitored Capital

events.title: Factor Score Construction
events.description: Define the universe, standardise metrics into z-scores, correct direction, decide on sector neutrality, and combine into a composite score (Chapter 3).

events.title: Point-in-Time Backtesting
events.description: Test the score against a bias-free, point-in-time dataset, screening for look-ahead bias, survivorship bias, and realistic transaction costs (Chapter 3).

events.title: Portfolio Construction
events.description: Decide long-only vs long-short given India's SLBM and F&O constraints, set rebalancing frequency, and choose a position-sizing approach (Chapter 3).

events.title: Paper Trading
events.description: Run the live decision process against real-time data through several full rebalance cycles, with no real capital at risk.

events.title: Phased Deployment
events.description: Start with a modest pilot allocation and scale up in stages as live results validate the backtest and paper-trading expectations.

events.title: Ongoing Monitoring
events.description: Track factor exposure drift, Effective N, and crowding proxies continuously, not just at rebalancing (earlier in Chapter 4).

events.title: Predefined Review
events.description: A written kill switch, agreed before deployment, triggers a formal strategy review if live performance breaches defined limits.

body.title: Before You Deploy Real Capital
steps: The strategy has been paper-traded through at least several full rebalance cycles with no unresolved operational issues
A phased capital deployment plan exists, with defined stages and criteria for increasing allocation
A live monitoring process tracks factor exposure, Effective N, and realised vs backtested performance on an ongoing basis, not only at rebalancing
A written kill switch defines, in advance, the exact conditions that trigger a formal strategy review
Crowding proxies, AUM growth into similar strategies, valuation spread compression, known index reconstitution dates, have been checked for the specific factor and universe being traded
Transaction cost assumptions used in the backtest have been validated against actual fills observed during paper trading

body.title: What Went Wrong Here?
body.scenario: A systematising trader builds a factor strategy, backtests it rigorously with point-in-time data, and is confident in the results. They deploy their full intended capital on day one, directly from backtest to live trading, with no paper trading period and no phased scaling. Three weeks in, they discover that their rebalancing process, which assumes all orders execute smoothly within an hour, actually takes most of a trading day to complete manually, causing several positions to be entered at prices meaningfully worse than the strategy's model assumed.
body.prompt: Which specific step from this lesson was skipped, and how would including it have caught this problem before real capital was at risk?
body.modelAnswer: The trader skipped paper trading. A rigorous, bias-free backtest, exactly as covered in Chapter 3, has no way to reveal that the actual, real-world process of placing dozens of orders manually takes most of a trading day rather than the hour the model assumes, because a backtest is a historical simulation, not a live operational rehearsal. Paper trading through even one or two full rebalance cycles, generating real orders against real-time data without committing capital, would have surfaced this exact timing mismatch immediately, since the trader would have observed how long their actual process takes under live conditions, and could have redesigned the rebalancing workflow or adjusted execution expectations before any real capital was exposed to it.

body.title: Test Yourself: The Purpose of a Kill Switch
body.question: Why should a strategy's kill switch criteria be written down and defined before the strategy goes live, rather than decided in the moment if losses occur?
options: It is a regulatory requirement for all systematic strategies in India
Deciding the exit criteria while calm, before any losses occur, protects against the same performance-chasing, emotionally-driven capitulation risk covered in Chapter 2
It guarantees the strategy will never experience a drawdown larger than expected
It removes the need for any ongoing exposure or performance monitoring
body.explanation: A kill switch decided in advance, while unemotional, is a defence against exactly the performance-chasing trap Chapter 2 described, capitulating on a strategy at the point of maximum pain because losses are being experienced in real time. Deciding the exit rule only after losses have already started risks making that same emotionally-driven mistake rather than following a predefined, disciplined process.

body.title: Vocabulary Check: Terms From This Lesson

cards.definition: Running a strategy's actual decision process against real-time data and generating real orders without committing real capital, to surface operational issues a backtest cannot reveal.
Starting a live strategy with a modest pilot allocation and increasing capital in stages as live results validate the backtest, rather than deploying full intended capital immediately.

A predefined, written rule specifying the exact conditions under which a live strategy will be paused, de-risked, or shut down, decided before deployment to avoid emotionally-driven decisions under pressure.

body.text: This lesson describes general implementation principles for educational purposes and is not a complete operational or compliance guide to running a live trading strategy. Running any systematic strategy with real capital involves regulatory, tax, and risk considerations specific to your situation; consult qualified professionals before deploying real money.

points: Paper trading, running the strategy's live decision process without real capital, catches operational problems a bias-free backtest structurally cannot see
Phased capital deployment keeps early mistakes cheap and directly tests whether a strategy's edge survives as deployed capital, and its market impact, grows
Live monitoring should continuously compare realised performance, exposure, and drawdown against backtest expectations, not just check in at each rebalance
A kill switch, written and agreed before going live, protects against the performance-chasing and capitulation risk covered in Chapter 2 by removing emotion from the exit decision

The full pipeline, from factor score construction through backtesting, portfolio construction, paper trading, phased deployment, and ongoing monitoring, is one continuous discipline, not a series of independent, disconnected steps

This closes the loop the course opened in Chapter 1: from Sharpe's single-factor CAPM in 1964 to a fully implemented, monitored, and risk-managed multi-factor strategy running on real capital in Indian markets today
